content: Breast stimulation has been proposed as a non-medical method to induce labor, offering women more autonomy over the induction process. This method has been evaluated for its effectiveness in promoting cervical ripening and labor induction during the third trimester, compared to either no intervention, placebo, or other induction methods. A systematic review included six clinical trials involving 719 women. When breast stimulation was compared to no intervention, there was a significant reduction in the number of women who were not in labor after 72 hours (62.7% versus 93.6%; relative risk [RR] 0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60 to 0.74). However, this effect was not observed in women with an unfavorable cervix. Additionally, breast stimulation was associated with a notable reduction in postpartum hemorrhage rates (0.7% versus 6%; RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.87). There was no significant difference in the rates of cesarean delivery (9% versus 10%; RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.38 to 2.12) or meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Importantly, no cases of uterine hyperstimulation were reported. However, three perinatal deaths occurred in the breast stimulation group (1.8% versus 0%; RR 8.17, 95% CI 0.45 to 147.77). When breast stimulation was compared to oxytocin alone, there was no significant difference in cesarean section rates (28% versus 47%; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.18). Similarly, no difference was observed in the number of women not in labor after 72 hours (58.8% versus 25%; RR 2.35, 95% CI 1.00 to 5.54) or in the rates of meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Four perinatal deaths were reported in the breast stimulation group (17.6% versus 5%; RR 3.53, 95% CI 0.40 to 30.88). The authors concluded that breast stimulation may be beneficial in reducing the number of women not in labor after 72 hours and in lowering postpartum hemorrhage rates. However, due to safety concerns, particularly in high-risk pregnancies, its use should be approached with caution until further research is conducted. Future studies should focus on evaluating its safety profile, including postpartum hemorrhage rates, labor induction success within 72 hours, and maternal satisfaction.
